li.a: Tablet Magazine: The Legacy of the Maalot Massacre
Unpacked: Ma'alot, 30 seconds that devastated a nation
iResearchNet: DFLP Attack on Ma'alot School
Jewish Telegraphic Agency: Documentary recalls the horrors of Ma'alot school massacre
World Jewish Congress: Palestinian terrorists kill 25 hostages in Ma'alot massacre
My Daily Kvetch: The Massacre in Maalot

content.p: In the small hours of 15 May 1974, three armed men who had crossed into Israel from Lebanon entered an elementary school in the northern town of Ma'alot, where more than 100 teenagers from a religious high school in Safed were sleeping on the floor. They held the group for most of a day, demanding the release of prisoners. At the end of the day a commando assault ended with the three attackers dead and 22 students killed in the classroom, in a rescue that the officer leading it said took 30 to 35 seconds. Sources differ on the full toll, which runs from 25 hostages to 28 people killed across the whole episode.

Ma'alot became a lasting reference point in Israeli memory. It came a few weeks after another deadly raid in Kiryat Shmona, with a caretaker government in office, and it exposed gaps in the police, the army and the school trip's own arrangements. It is also remembered through street names, kindergartens and a school that carry the victims' names.

The group came from the Amit school in Safed, a religious school whose pupils, according to a Safed teacher quoted by Tablet, were from North African immigrant families. On 14 May 1974 two buses, a large van and a car set out from the city for a three-day outing of hiking and sleeping outdoors, a program run under the Gadna youth corps. Near Moshav Avdon, Tablet reports, soldiers stopped the convoy and said terrorists had been reported infiltrating from Lebanon.

Unpacked describes the north of the country as being on high alert, so the students and teachers were redirected at the last minute to sleep indoors somewhere safer. The detailed account on the My Daily Kvetch blog adds that the group's leader checked by telephone with the Gadna commissioner in Haifa, who allowed the trip to continue, and that the police later asked for the pupils to spend the night in the Netiv Meir school instead of a field. That school, in the centre of Ma'alot, should have been empty. According to the Unpacked account, the boys slept on the first floor and the girls on the second.
content.h2: The three men and the first killings
content.p: Unpacked and the My Daily Kvetch blog say the attackers belonged to the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, a Marxist group that had split from the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine in 1969. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency and the World Jewish Congress both name the Popular Front instead; the other pages, including iResearchNet, give the Democratic Front.

The My Daily Kvetch account says all three were born in Israel or the area then under its control: Ali al-Atmah, born in Haifa, aged 27; Muhammad Dardour, born in Beit Hanina, aged 20; and Ziyad Ka'ik, born in Taibe, aged 22, who it says spoke fluent Hebrew and led the group. Unpacked likewise says two of the three were Israeli Arabs from Haifa. Neither attacker was tried, because all three died at the school.

Unpacked says the three men spent the previous day hiding in a cave and moved by night. The first people they met were Arab Israelis. A van carrying women home from a Kiryat Ata garment factory was fired on on the road above Ma'alot, at about 10:45 p.m. according to the blog and just before midnight according to Unpacked. The sources differ on the result. Unpacked says one woman died and every other passenger was wounded. The blog names her as Hasibah Shalala, aged 27, from the village of Fassuta, and says seven were wounded and the driver was hurt. iResearchNet says two women died, one at once and one after the driver got the van to safety. Unpacked reports that the police sent to the scene believed the attack was the whole of the raid and concentrated their search near the border.

The three men went on into Ma'alot. They reached an apartment block where a light was on, and shot dead Yosef and Fortuna Cohen and their four-year-old son Eliahu. The World Jewish Congress and iResearchNet say the couple's five-year-old daughter Miriam was wounded and survived and that their 16-month-old son Yitzhak was unhurt. According to iResearchNet the attackers then asked a sanitation worker, Yaakov Kadosh, for directions and beat and shot him, believing he was dead. Tablet adds that a sculpture near the Founders Museum in Ma'alot honours the Cohen family.

Accounts of the time of entry vary: 3:30 a.m. (Unpacked), "before dawn" (iResearchNet) and about 5 a.m. (Tablet). iResearchNet says the attackers shouted in Arabic and Hebrew and took charge of the sleeping group. A teacher quoted by Unpacked remembered pounding on a door, then shouting for everyone to jump out of the window. Unpacked says the boys on the first floor had the easier escape, and many got out. iResearchNet counts seventeen students, the driver and two army escorts who escaped; Unpacked says about 85 students, two teachers and the medic remained. Tablet adds that nearly all of the Amit teachers left by a back door after the infiltration, a failure criticised by Bezalel Dahan, then a teacher in Safed, who said "You can't abandon kids."

The attackers herded the hostages into one classroom and rigged it with explosives. Survivor Shula Binyamin-Rubin told Unpacked they were first forbidden to speak or to use the toilet, and that later the attackers took them three at a time to a corridor window and fired between their feet so they would cry out to the government. Tzipi Maimon-Bokris, later photographed being carried clear, told the JTA documentary that the children begged the attackers not to kill them and that one answered that they would soon be soldiers and had to be stopped. Eli Amar told Tablet that when he asked a hostage-taker why they had done it, the man pressed a weapon to his head and told him he would never have children or grandchildren.

iResearchNet says the attackers later freed a medic, Narkiss Mordechai, with letters addressed to the French and Romanian ambassadors, asking them to act as intermediaries. The demand was the release of 23 prisoners and three other detainees, among them Kozo Okamoto, a Japanese Red Army member jailed over the Lod airport shootings. The note set a 6 p.m. deadline, said the school was rigged with explosives and required a code word to be sent from the freed men once they reached Damascus or Nicosia. Unpacked puts the figures at between 20 and 26 prisoners.

iResearchNet describes the attackers' leader appearing at a window from 9 a.m. with five students, firing and throwing grenades; a local man who was on army leave died from a stray bullet. The initial government negotiator, it says, was Victor Cohen of the security service. In one of her last hours, a 15-year-old pupil named Ilana Turgeman, whom some sources call Ilana Ne'eman, wrote a letter to her parents dated 11:25 a.m., which Unpacked quotes in full.

Unpacked notes that Golda Meir had resigned the month before, and that her cabinet, still in office until a new government took over in June, had to decide. It says she was willing to negotiate, saying one does not wage war on the backs of children, while Dayan argued for killing the attackers and freeing the students. Levin, who commanded the assault, says in the documentary, as JTA reports it, that the conflict that day was between Dayan, who wanted decisive action, and Gur, who preferred caution. The My Daily Kvetch blog says Gur asked for the negotiations to go on and for the cabinet to approve any raid, and that only two ministers, Yosef Burg and Moshe Kol, voted against military action.

The details differ. Unpacked says the cabinet debated for fourteen hours and the Knesset eventually agreed to the demands, even bringing 20 prisoners to the area, blindfolded and bound; by some accounts, it says, that was when the attackers began to dismantle their explosives. iResearchNet says the top three prisoners on the list were moved from prison toward Ma'alot, that the idea of the French ambassador going to the school was refused, and that the attackers said anyone approaching without the code word would be shot. The blog says a decision to negotiate was reached by 4 p.m. but the attackers refused more time. The World Jewish Congress says only that the government asked for more time and was refused.

Sayeret Matkal was flown in at dawn, the blog says, and took up positions around the school. The blog has Gur arriving at 7 a.m. and Dayan at 7:30; iResearchNet also has both men at Ma'alot overseeing the operation. The time of the assault is given variously: 5:25 p.m. as the order and about 5:30 as the start (blog), 5:40 p.m. (iResearchNet) and about fifteen minutes before the deadline (Unpacked).

Unpacked says the first team through the front doors came under fire and threw a phosphorus grenade, whose smoke blinded the snipers and sent the second team to the wrong floor. The blog says the team under Levin ran up to an empty floor before coming back to the hall where the children were held, and that Ka'ik was shot at the classroom doorway. It describes al-Atmah continuing to fire into the crowd after being hit, then throwing grenades. Hostages jumped from windows. Amar, according to Tablet, pulled up a classmate, then a second and a third, onto a window ledge and pushed them out before jumping himself; another student who jumped was killed, and one of those he helped, Dina Yakuti, was hit as she landed but recovered.

"The whole operation took 30, 35 seconds," Levin says in the documentary. "If we'd been able to do it in 10, how many more could we have saved?" iResearchNet notes that soldiers came in through various entrances and windows and that confusion followed. The three attackers were killed.

The World Jewish Congress reports 25 hostages killed, including 22 children, and 68 wounded. JTA gives 22 killed and 68 gravely wounded. Unpacked counts 26 people dead, among them 22 students under 17, and writes of 26 caskets at the funerals the next day. Tablet speaks of 28 Israelis killed near and in Ma'alot, including the 22 students. The totals depend on whether the Cohen family, the woman from the van and others killed during the day are counted.

The World Jewish Congress says Meir told the Knesset five days later that a commission of inquiry would be created. The blog gives 20 May 1974 as the date it was appointed, headed by reserve major general Amos Horev. It says the commission found the police rules on school trips had been grossly mishandled: one police district did not have to tell another about trips it had approved, and so the northern district had no full picture. It also says the Meona station commander responsible for Ma'alot had held the post under six months and had no phone at home, and that nobody in higher police ranks accepted responsibility for warning him of the tension on the border. Moshe Givati, a veteran of the rescue force, is quoted by the blog asking on the fortieth anniversary where the army, police and the group's escorts had been in the seven hours after the first shooting.

Tablet says the failure to rescue the hostages safely led to the creation of Yamam, a hostage-rescue unit under the police, and that the episode broke the taboo against negotiating with kidnappers. Efraim Inbar of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security called Ma'alot "a big debacle", though he added that decisive action is generally better than yielding to demands.

The memory remains close to the ground. Tablet describes a Safed intersection signposted with both "22 Children of Tzfat" and "22 Children of Maalot" names, 22 kindergartens named for plants and animals, a rebuilt Amit school now named for the 22, a stained-glass window with their names and a memorial room in the Ma'alot school itself. A Reform synagogue in Irvine, California, renamed itself Shir Ha-Ma'alot in 1975. In 2011 the American filmmaker Brandon Assanti released a documentary, "Their Eyes Were Dry", which an Israeli consulate spokeswoman told JTA was, as far as she knew, the first full-length film about the events. The survivor Dina Yakuti told Tablet that for twenty years she did not discuss what she lived through except in therapy.
